PHASE 6 · EVIDENCE-BASED PRACTICE & PROFESSIONAL FNP PRACTICE

Week 139 — Lesson 163: Emergency Preparedness, Disaster Response & Climate-Related Health

FNP-level goal: Protect patients and communities before, during, and after emergencies by recognizing hazards early, maintaining essential primary care, working within incident command, triaging safely under constrained conditions, communicating accurately, and reducing unequal disaster impact without practicing outside competence or authority.

Learning Objectives

  • Apply an all-hazards framework across prevention, protection, mitigation, response, and recovery.
  • Explain the FNP role within incident command, emergency operations, public health, healthcare coalitions, and community partnerships.
  • Identify patient, clinic, workforce, supply, data, medication, utility, and referral vulnerabilities before an incident.
  • Prioritize immediate threats, time-sensitive care, continuity needs, and appropriate escalation during resource disruption.
  • Develop risk-specific plans for heat, wildfire smoke, poor air quality, flood, power outage, infectious threats, displacement, and behavioral-health consequences.
  • Use ethical, equitable, accessible, trauma-informed, and culturally responsive communication and resource-allocation processes.
  • Evaluate drills and real incidents through after-action review, corrective action, and recovery measures.

Part 1 — What Counts as an Emergency?

An emergency is not defined only by dramatic images or a formal declaration. It exists when demand, hazard, or disruption threatens health and exceeds—or is likely to exceed—ordinary capability. A prolonged power outage, cyberattack, heat wave, medication shortage, wildfire smoke event, infectious outbreak, flood, earthquake, or evacuation can all compromise primary care.

For the FNP, the central questions are: What threatens life now? Which essential services are failing? Who is most vulnerable to that failure? What can this team safely do, and which incident, emergency, public-health, or referral pathway must be activated?

Part 2 — The All-Hazards Approach

An all-hazards approach builds common capabilities that apply across events: leadership, communication, situational awareness, triage, continuity, infection prevention, resource tracking, workforce safety, patient movement, documentation, and recovery. Hazard-specific annexes add details such as decontamination, smoke protection, evacuation, or cold-chain management.

One plan cannot predict every event. It should define how the organization detects change, activates authority, assigns roles, obtains information, communicates, protects people, and adapts as conditions evolve.

Part 3 — The Five Mission Areas

Preparedness extends across prevention, protection, mitigation, response, and recovery. Prevention and protection reduce the chance or impact of threats. Mitigation reduces vulnerability before the event. Response saves life, stabilizes the incident, and meets basic needs. Recovery restores and improves clinical, social, and community function.

Primary care participates in all five: vaccination and infection prevention; protecting data and medications; identifying home oxygen or insulin vulnerability; staffing alternate workflows; and restoring chronic, preventive, mental-health, and rehabilitation care after the acute phase.

Part 4 — Risk Is Hazard × Exposure × Vulnerability

A hazard becomes clinically important through exposure and vulnerability. The same heat wave creates different risk for a healthy adult with air conditioning and an older adult living alone with heart failure, diuretics, mobility limitation, and no reliable cooling or transportation.

Assess who is exposed, how intensely and for how long, which protective resources exist, and which conditions increase susceptibility. Avoid describing people as inherently vulnerable when policy, infrastructure, access, discrimination, or resource distribution creates much of the risk.

Part 5 — Build a Hazard Vulnerability Assessment

List plausible natural, infectious, technological, infrastructure, security, supply, and human-caused hazards. Estimate likelihood, severity, warning time, duration, patient impact, staff impact, property and utility impact, supply dependence, and current capability. Include community and partner knowledge.

Use the assessment to prioritize mitigation and exercises. A coastal clinic, a rural practice dependent on one road, and an urban clinic serving high-rise residents with elevator-dependent mobility will require different operational details.

Part 6 — Map Essential Clinical Functions

Identify services that cannot safely stop: urgent triage, medication refills with high withdrawal or decompensation risk, anticoagulation or other critical monitoring, pregnancy warning-sign assessment, insulin and oxygen continuity, infectious-disease response, result management, referral escalation, and communication with medically fragile patients.

For each function, define maximum tolerable downtime, minimum staffing, supplies, data, space, utilities, communication, backup site, partner support, and recovery sequence. Not every routine service has equal urgency.

Part 7 — Continuity of Operations

A continuity plan explains how essential functions continue when the usual clinic, workforce, EHR, laboratory, pharmacy, power, internet, telephone, or referral network is disrupted. Include succession of authority, alternate workflows, emergency contacts, remote or alternate sites, patient notification, and return-to-normal criteria.

Paper downtime processes require secure forms, patient identification, medication and allergy verification, result tracking, documentation ownership, and later reconciliation into the record. Temporary workarounds must not become undocumented parallel systems.

Part 8 — Incident Command and Role Clarity

FEMA's National Incident Management System provides common concepts, terminology, resource management, and coordination. The Incident Command System organizes authority and functions so people do not self-deploy or issue conflicting instructions. A clinic may work within an organizational incident structure even when it does not command the broader event.

Know who has incident authority, who supervises you, how assignments are received, where safety concerns are reported, how resources are requested, and which communication channels are official. Clinical seniority does not automatically equal incident command.

Part 9 — Command, Operations, Planning, Logistics, and Finance

Incident structures commonly separate command from operations, planning, logistics, and finance or administration. Clinical care generally falls under operations; planning develops situational awareness and action plans; logistics obtains people and supplies; finance tracks time, contracts, costs, and claims.

The exact structure scales to the incident. The important principle is span of control, clear accountability, common objectives, and documented resource requests—not memorizing a chart while bypassing the actual chain of command.

Part 10 — Situational Awareness

Situational awareness combines what happened, what is happening, what may happen next, and what capabilities remain. Use verified sources: emergency management, public health, weather and air-quality agencies, utilities, healthcare coalitions, organizational leaders, and direct operational data.

Track patient demand, acuity, staff availability, supply burn rate, power and communications, laboratory and pharmacy function, referral capacity, facility safety, and community access. Mark uncertain information and update it rather than presenting estimates as facts.

Part 11 — Activation Levels and Triggers

Predefine triggers for enhanced monitoring, partial activation, full activation, service reduction, closure, shelter-in-place, evacuation, or relocation. Examples include unsafe indoor temperature, loss of water, failed medication refrigeration, staffing below safe minimums, inaccessible roads, credible threat, overwhelming demand, or public-health direction.

A trigger should name who decides and how the decision is communicated. Waiting until every variable is certain can make evacuation or continuity impossible.

Part 12 — Triage: Acuity Before Convenience

During surge, triage identifies immediate threats and the safest next destination. Assess airway, breathing, circulation, neurologic status, severe pain or injury, pregnancy emergencies, exposure, infection risk, and time-sensitive chronic conditions. Reassess because status and capacity change.

Do not invent a disaster triage system during the event. Use the validated system and jurisdictional or organizational protocol for the setting, train beforehand, document category and reassessment, and ensure that triage is not mistaken for a complete medical evaluation.

Part 13 — Conventional, Contingency, and Crisis Conditions

Conventional care uses usual spaces, staff, and standards. Contingency strategies adapt resources while aiming for functionally equivalent care. Crisis conditions involve severe scarcity and require formally authorized strategies that may substantially change care delivery.

Individual clinicians should not silently declare crisis standards. Follow authorized plans, ethics and legal guidance, incident leadership, and transparent allocation processes. Return toward conventional care as soon as capability allows.

Part 14 — Ethical Allocation Under Scarcity

Resource allocation should use relevant, consistently applied criteria; procedural fairness; transparency appropriate to the situation; disability and civil-rights protections; conflict management; reassessment; and an appeal or review pathway when feasible. Bedside clinicians need support so allocation is not reduced to improvised personal judgment.

Do not use social worth, wealth, influence, race, disability stereotypes, or first-come-first-served convenience without examining how access barriers distort opportunity. Separate allocation decisions from discrimination and document the authorized process.

Part 15 — Workforce Safety

Healthcare workers face infectious, chemical, smoke, heat, ergonomic, violence, fatigue, and psychological hazards. Use appropriate PPE, fit testing where required, exposure protocols, buddy systems, rest, hydration, safe staffing, security, and stop-work authority for imminent danger.

A professional duty to care is not an unlimited duty to accept preventable harm or work beyond competence. Report symptoms and exposures, avoid self-deployment, and use trained response roles.

Part 16 — Infection Prevention During Disruption

Crowding, sheltering, limited ventilation, water disruption, and supply scarcity can increase transmission. Maintain hand hygiene, respiratory precautions, environmental cleaning, ventilation, separation when indicated, appropriate PPE, safe specimen handling, and current isolation guidance.

Screen for epidemiologic links and unusual clusters. Coordinate testing, prophylaxis, treatment, vaccination, reporting, and risk communication with infection prevention and public health. Avoid using scarce antibiotics or antivirals without an evidence-based indication.

Part 17 — Medication Continuity

Prioritize medications whose interruption can cause rapid harm: insulin, antiseizure therapy, corticosteroids in dependent patients, anticoagulants or antithrombotics when indicated, transplant or other immunosuppression, selected psychiatric medications, opioid-use-disorder treatment, and oxygen-related therapies. Exact priority depends on the patient and event.

Verify identity, indication, dose, allergies, organ function, interactions, current supply, storage, and available substitute. Emergency refill and controlled-substance rules vary; use current law, payer, pharmacy, and organizational policy rather than making informal promises.

Part 18 — Cold Chain and Temperature-Sensitive Products

Vaccines, biologics, insulin, and other products may be damaged by temperature excursions. Know which refrigerators are monitored, backup power and transport options, responsible personnel, temperature logs, quarantine procedures, manufacturer or public-health consultation, and documentation.

Do not assume appearance proves potency and do not discard or administer affected stock without authorized guidance. Protect the chain of custody and keep patient communication accurate.

Part 19 — Power-Dependent Medical Needs

Identify patients dependent on oxygen concentrators, ventilatory support, dialysis, infusion, refrigerated medication, powered mobility, communication devices, elevators, or electrically powered feeding equipment. Confirm backup batteries, charging, vendor support, emergency contacts, transportation, and destination planning.

A registry can support outreach, but it may be incomplete or outdated and must be protected. Patients remain partners in planning; registration never guarantees immediate rescue.

Part 20 — Extreme Heat

Heat can worsen cardiovascular, renal, respiratory, metabolic, pregnancy, and medication-related risk. Assess exposure, exertion, hydration, cooling access, housing, work, cognition, medications, and symptoms. Heat stroke—hyperthermia with central nervous system dysfunction—is a medical emergency requiring immediate cooling and emergency care.

Help patients create a heat action plan based on current local guidance. Fans may not provide safe cooling at very high indoor temperatures. Review whether diuretics, anticholinergic burden, sedatives, stimulants, or other therapies alter risk, but do not advise unsupervised discontinuation.

Part 21 — Wildfire Smoke and Air Quality

Wildfire smoke can worsen asthma, COPD, cardiovascular disease, pregnancy risk, and other chronic conditions. Use current air-quality information, assess respiratory and cardiac symptoms, update action plans and prescriptions, and address indoor air filtration, evacuation capability, occupational exposure, and access to properly fitted respiratory protection when recommended.

Severe dyspnea, chest pain, hypoxemia, altered mental status, suspected inhalation injury, or failure of usual rescue treatment requires urgent or emergency evaluation. A cloth covering or loose surgical mask should not be represented as equivalent to a well-fitting particulate respirator.

Part 22 — Floods, Storms, and Water Disruption

Flood events create drowning, trauma, electrocution, carbon monoxide, contaminated water, mold, infection, medication loss, displacement, and interrupted dialysis or refrigeration risks. Avoid entering moving water and warn against indoor generator or grill use.

After exposure, evaluate wounds, tetanus status, toxic exposure, respiratory symptoms, gastrointestinal illness, and chronic-care disruption. Use official boil-water, reentry, food-safety, and cleanup guidance.

Part 23 — Carbon Monoxide

Carbon monoxide is odorless and can cause headache, dizziness, nausea, weakness, confusion, syncope, chest pain, or death. Multiple ill people in the same location, symptoms that improve away, or generator, heater, vehicle, or fire exposure should raise suspicion.

Remove the person from exposure without endangering rescuers, activate emergency evaluation, provide oxygen and testing per protocol, and contact poison-control or emergency authorities. A normal pulse oximeter reading does not exclude carbon monoxide poisoning.

Part 24 — Cyberattack and EHR Downtime

A cyber incident can affect scheduling, identity verification, medication history, orders, results, imaging, communication, billing, and connected devices. Follow downtime and security protocols; do not connect personal media, create unofficial cloud files, or transmit protected data through unapproved channels.

Use minimum necessary data, independent medication and allergy verification, read-back for critical communication, manual result logs, and reconciliation after restoration. Report suspicious messages or device behavior promptly.

Part 25 — Evacuation and Shelter-in-Place

The safest choice depends on the hazard, building integrity, time, transportation, patient acuity, route, destination, and official direction. Preplan patient movement, mobility and sensory accommodations, medication and oxygen transport, records, family reunification, staff accountability, and receiving-facility handoff.

Never block fire or emergency routes with clinic supplies. During shelter-in-place, maintain air, water, sanitation, security, temperature, medications, communication, and a threshold for abandoning the plan if conditions worsen.

Part 26 — Accessible and Equitable Preparedness

Plans must include people with disabilities, limited English proficiency, low literacy, unstable housing, incarceration or institutional residence, immigration concerns, rural isolation, limited transportation, caregiving duties, and digital exclusion. Provide accessible formats, qualified interpreters, mobility support, and trusted communication routes.

Do not require a smartphone, car, English fluency, formal address, or government identification unless truly necessary. Assess whether alerts, shelters, evacuation transport, medication access, and recovery funds reach the people at greatest risk.

Part 27 — Risk Communication

Communicate what is known, unknown, changing, and actionable. Lead with the most important protective action, use plain language, name the source and update time, provide alternatives for different access needs, and correct errors visibly.

Avoid false reassurance, unsupported certainty, blame, sensationalism, and repeated technical language without meaning. Coordinate with incident communication so patients do not receive conflicting instructions.

Part 28 — Misinformation and Trust

During uncertainty, rumors fill information gaps. Listen for the underlying fear or experience, acknowledge uncertainty, provide a concise correction and evidence, explain what would change the recommendation, and direct patients to current trusted sources.

Trust is built before the incident through respectful care, community partnership, transparency, and follow-through. Do not shame patients or dismiss legitimate historical reasons for distrust.

Part 29 — Behavioral Health and Psychological First Aid

Disasters can cause acute stress, grief, sleep disruption, substance use, depression, anxiety, family conflict, and worsening serious mental illness. Assess immediate safety, suicidality, psychosis, intoxication or withdrawal, medication interruption, child and elder protection, and functional supports.

Provide calm, practical, trauma-informed support; connect basic needs and social supports; avoid forcing detailed trauma narration; and refer or escalate based on risk. Monitor responders as well as patients.

Part 30 — Recovery Is a Clinical Phase

After the visible emergency, patients may face lost housing, employment, medication, mobility, records, caregivers, and trust. Delayed complications include wound infection, uncontrolled chronic illness, missed cancer or prenatal care, post-traumatic symptoms, financial toxicity, and disrupted development or schooling.

Use registries and partner outreach to restore priority care. Recovery should reduce previous vulnerabilities rather than simply recreate an unsafe baseline.

Part 31 — Exercises and After-Action Improvement

Use discussion-based and operational exercises to test roles, communications, downtime, evacuation, triage, supply, and partner coordination. Include realistic access and equity challenges. Define objectives and safety rules before the exercise.

After an exercise or incident, document what was expected, what occurred, why gaps appeared, what worked, and which corrective action has an owner, deadline, resource, and verification method. An after-action report without completed improvement is not preparedness.

Part 32 — The FNP as Preparedness Leader

The FNP understands which interruptions cause rapid clinical harm across the lifespan. They can translate hazard information into patient action plans, identify high-risk registries, protect medication continuity, improve accessible communication, participate in incident operations, and advocate for mitigation.

The FNP must stay within assigned authority and competence, maintain patient confidentiality, report required conditions and hazards, and request emergency, specialty, public-health, toxicology, environmental, occupational, security, or legal expertise early.

Clinical Case 1 — Heat, Power Loss, and Heart Failure

A regional heat emergency causes a three-day outage. An older adult with HFpEF, CKD, diabetes, limited mobility, and no air conditioning reports weakness and dizziness. The FNP assesses for heat illness, volume status, glucose abnormality, renal injury, medication effects, and emergency red flags rather than advising indiscriminate fluid intake.

The team uses its power-dependence and high-risk registry, confirms a safe cooling destination and transportation, coordinates medication and glucose-monitoring continuity, provides clear escalation instructions, and tracks whether the patient actually reaches support. Aggregate failures inform future mitigation.

Clinical Case 2 — Wildfire Smoke and Clinic Surge

Smoke causes a surge of cough, wheeze, chest symptoms, and refill requests. The clinic activates an incident workflow: one verified message, symptom triage, separate emergency criteria, pharmacy and supply tracking, outreach to patients with asthma or COPD, interpreter access, staffing relief, and coordination with local air-quality and public-health sources.

A patient with chest pressure and severe dyspnea is not routed into a routine refill queue. The FNP recognizes potential cardiopulmonary emergency and escalates immediately while the broader team continues population messaging and continuity care.

Clinical Case 3 — Cyber Downtime

The EHR and electronic prescribing system are unavailable. A patient requests insulin and reports multiple medication allergies, but the current list cannot be viewed. Staff feel pressure to guess from memory.

The FNP uses the approved downtime process, independently verifies the patient and regimen through available authoritative sources, assesses current glucose and supply, documents on the secure downtime form, communicates with read-back, tracks the prescription, and ensures reconciliation after restoration. The team does not create a personal spreadsheet or send protected information through private messaging.

FNP High-Yield Framework: READY

  1. R — Recognize the hazard and immediate threats: Life safety, exposure, incident status, and people at disproportionate risk.
  2. E — Establish command, communication, and essential functions: Assigned role, verified information, continuity priorities, and activation triggers.
  3. A — Adapt care using authorized plans: Triage, infection control, medication continuity, accessible communication, and resource stewardship.
  4. D — Document, disclose uncertainty, and defend equity: Decisions, reassessment, privacy, fair allocation, accommodations, and reporting.
  5. Y — Yield learning into recovery: Restore care, address delayed harm, complete corrective actions, and build back safer.

Take-Home Summary

Preparedness is a continuous clinical and systems responsibility, not a binder opened after disaster. Use an all-hazards plan with hazard-specific details; define essential functions and downtime workflows; work through incident command; protect patients, staff, data, medication, and utilities; and distinguish conventional, contingency, and formally authorized crisis conditions. Address heat, smoke, flood, power, infectious, toxic, cyber, displacement, and behavioral-health risks with current guidance. Communication, allocation, evacuation, and recovery must be accessible and equitable. Exercise the plan, complete corrective actions, and use recovery to reduce future vulnerability.

Educational note: Follow current FEMA NIMS and local emergency-management structures, CDC and health-department clinical and public-health guidance, HHS/ASPR and healthcare-coalition plans, OSHA/NIOSH workplace protections, poison-control and environmental-health guidance, and organizational emergency, security, privacy, infection-control, medication, evacuation, and downtime policies. Incident authority, reporting, emergency prescribing, allocation, and scope rules vary by jurisdiction and event; this lesson is educational and does not replace certified emergency-response training or authorized incident direction.
